text: The assembly will hear an address by his
excellency
Lord Faka,
Prime Minister of the Kingdom of Tonga.
I request protocol to escort his
excellency and invite him to address the
assembly.
Mr. President, the general assembly,
your excellencies, ladies and gentlemen,
I bring you warm greetings from His
Majesty King Dubo V 6 and the people of
the Kingdom of Tonga.
Nine months into my service as prime
minister, I stand here mindful that
Pacific leaders have come before me,
raising the same warnings, making the
same appeals.
Today, I'm compelled to make them again.
The question before us is not whether
the world has heard our message, but why
has it still not acted?
We live in a world more connected than
ever, but greater connection has not
bought greater unity.
We meet amid deepening division,
geopolitical conflict, and competition.
For Tonga, navigating such stormy
currents is not new. As descendants of
voyages, we have been in the survival
business much longer than most have
appreciated.
Under King George I, Tonga preserved its
independence during an era of colonial
expansion.
Our Constitution of 1875
secured Towin's rights and freedoms over
seven decades before the Universal
Declaration of Human Rights.
It reflects our fierce determination to
chart our own course.
That is the essence of our sovereignty.
Multilateralism
allows us to project the power of our
ideas rather than the might of our
power.
Tonga participates as an equal under the
founding principles of the United
Nations Charter, the sovereign equality
of states.
This is how we must approach our theme.
Restoring trust, managing
transformation,
a united nation that delivers for all.
Enduring trust is restored when
commitments produce results.
True transformation is realized when our
communities, economies, and ecosystems
can anticipate change and recover with
greater strength.
The small line developing states must
not bear the disproportionate costs of
the challenges they did little to
create.
Mr. President, too much of our
international architecture still
reflects the world of 1945
rather than today's realities.
If the United Nations is to remain the
principal vehicle through which
sovereign nations confront global
challenges, it must transform.
We need a United Nations that enables
innovation.
One that expands meaningful access to
investment and technology, especially
for the islands, developing countries
who are too often excluded from both.
We need a stronger general assembly and
institutions that respond effectively to
the needs of the majority of our
members.
We cannot keep negotiating climate,
biodiversity, and the ocean and separate
cops when they are clearly an
interconnected ecosystem requiring
integrated and coherent solutions.
We call on global processes to recognize
the ocean climate nexus and address
these interconnected challenges
together.
We need a more inclusive security
council equipped for today's challenges.
A security council that recognizes the
triple planetary crisis as a profound
threat to peace and security.
We need a financial architecture that
delivers timely and accessible financing
to those who most need them.
Internationally,
pledge commitments must be actioned
urgently.
The next secretary general must
understand these realities intimately.
It is in this spirit that Tong has
nominated Ambassador Ivon Baky of
Ecuador, whose vision for a renewed
reformed United Nations speaks to the
needs of vulnerable states.
To restore trust, every member state,
large or small, must have a voice in
shaping this organization's future and a
stake in its success.
Mr. President, your excellencies,
the Pacific region spans onethird of the
Earth's surface. It is our home. Through
the 2050 strategy for the blue Pacific
continent, we have set our own course
and identified our thematic priorities.
For Tonga, investing in the ocean and
nature is foundational in achieving its
development ambition.
Protecting and restoring them builds our
climate resilience. It strengthens our
food security and enables a sta
sustainable blue economy.
The financing and partnerships we build
around ocean and nature-based solutions
will help determine our future and
sustain our people.
Mr. President, we have declared our
region an ocean of peace in 2025.
It sends a clear message. The Pacific
must not become a staging ground for
military escalation
or a battleground for major power
rivalry.
However, our ocean of peace is more than
the absence of conflict.
Our most pressing threats already
reaching our shores. Transnational
crime, illicit drugs, illegal,
unregulated, and unreported fishing.
Cyber threats and unresolved
consequences of nuclear testing and
radioactive contamination remain.
In this respect, our region is committed
to directly utilizing innovative
technologies and working closely with
our trusted security partners to address
our security challenges.
We are committed to protecting the
rights of marginalized people and ending
violence against women and young girls.
This year, Tonga ratified United Nations
Convention on Rights of Persons with
Disabilities,
reaffirming our commitment to the
dignity and the equal participation of
persons with disabilities.
We also aceded to the treaty on the
non-prololiferation of nuclear weapons
and ratified the comprehensive nuclear
testban treaty. In doing so, we
completed the universal universalization
of the CTBT in the Pacific.
On climate, the Pacific is already
drowning in a crisis, a crisis that
others continue to postpone addressing.
UNEP's limiting overshoot report warns
that exceeding 1.5 degrees Celsius could
occur within the next few years. But
crossing that threshold must not become
an excuse for abandoning it. We must
peak as low as possible and return below
1.5 degrees Celsius as quickly as
possible.
Every fraction of a degree matters.
The Pacific loses an estimated of $500
million every year due to natural
disasters such as cyclones, flooding.
Early warning systems give communities
time to prepare and reduce these losses.
That may be a modest sum in global
terms, but for Pacific nations, it is a
heavy toll on our countries and our
people. And yet the financing to prevent
such losses still falls short. The
Pacific Resiliency Facility, our own
financing mechanism for building
community resilience, needs a further
328 million in pledges to reach its
initial capitalization target of $500
million.
Weather Ready Pacific, designed to
reduce the human and economic costs of
severe weather events, needs a further
160 million to reach its target.
Tonga's climate trust fund, a direct
community fund, which dispersed its
first round of grants this year, also
requires significant funding support.
We call on all all our partners to
invest in these Pacific designed and
Pacific owned solutions.
Tonga stands behind 2,26 Pacific Island
foreign leaders, the Balau declaration,
and calls on all our major emitters to
act urgently.
Climate action is a legal obligation,
but meeting those obligations will
require difficult decisions rooted in
science.
Climate leadership is not a popularity
contest.
Seven of the nine planetary boundaries
have been breached by human activity.
Climate action is not an option. Tonga
is accelerating its transition away from
fossil fuels and expanding renewable
energy. And we encourage the shift to
electric vehicles.
For us, decarbonizing
also means greater energy security and
protection from global for fuel price
shocks.
We must phase out the explicit fossil
fuel subsidies estimated by the IMF at
725 billion.
International financial institutions and
multilateral development banks must
recognize the multi-dimensional
vulnerability index, the MVI,
which ensures that it informs
eligibility and allocations.
By any credible index, Tong is amongst
the world's most vulnerable countries.
However, we call on all nations,
especially the world's largest emitters,
to attend the pre-OP 31 meetings in Fiji
and Touvalu in October this year.
Come to the Pacific and confront what
1.5 degrees means for our water, our
people, our food, our homes, and our
security.
We welcome the general assembly's
declaration on sea level rise, a
significant achievement for the
preservation of sovereignty.
It marks the first time all member
states have agreed on a single common
text on sea level rise.
Our resilience account for every hazard,
including geohhazards confronting our
islands.
Over the last few years, Tonga has
endured cyclones, flooding, earthquakes,
and tsunamis.
This year, the super El Nino currently
forming over the Pacific Ocean further
intensifies weather patterns,
compounding the pressures on our people.
We therefore need integrated warning and
response systems that can protect our
communities against the full range of
planetary risks.
Tong has committed to protecting at
least 30% of our ocean by 2030. Our
ratification of the BB&J agreement
extends that commitment beyond our
waters, supporting the protection of
marine biodiversity on the high seas.
Our task is to navigate a course that
safeguards the ocean and unlocks its
value to our people. This principle
underpins Tonga's ocean strategy.
It is in that spirit that we intend to
convene a Polynesian Ocean Summit in
Tonga May of 2027
to move from shared ambition to
practical action.
But our responsibility does not stop at
the boundaries of our Pacific continent.
Consider the humpback whales. Born in
Tonga's warm oceans, it migrates to
Antarctica to feed on krill before
returning to the Pacific to escape the
winter and breed.
Tonga's sanctuary protects them, but
their survival depends on healthy
ecosystems at both ends of that journey.
What happens in the southern seas of
Antarctica is felt in the southern
oceans of Tonga.
So we invite partners to join us in
Tonga with practical commitments that
recognize the scale and
interconnectedness of our shared ocean
corridors.
Mr. President,
the same principle extends across our
development. Interconnection must not be
dependency
for Tonga. Resilience means taking
greater control of the forces shaping
our future and turning the resources
within our geography into greater
self-sufficiency.
When we import fossil fuels, we also
import their volatility.
Moving away from them is therefore both
a climate imperative and an energy
security necessity.
Tonga is not short of ambition.
70% renewable energy by 2030, 100%
renewable energy by 2035.
However, the forces shaping our future
are not solely environmental or
economic. They're increasingly
technological.
Mr. President, digital connectivity and
rapid technology advancements are
transforming how we live. They offer
significant opportunities for big ocean
sovereign states. boss,
but they also risk creating new
inequalities and dependencies.
Those who benefit last from global
change often bear its highest costs. We
continue to live with that injustice
through climate change. We cannot again
be asked to adapt only after systems
have been built and the rules written.
For Tonga, submarine cables and
satellite links are foundational
infrastructures that connect our islands
to global opportunities. But
connectivity alone is not enough.
Digital skills and secure, resilient
systems must support it. And we will
protect our children online and retain
sovereignty over our national data.
Tonga does not need to be first in
artificial intelligence,
quantum computing, or every technology
that follows. But Tonga will not simply
endure global transformations. It will
exercise sovereignty by helping shape
the rules and norms around it.
Tonga is looking beyond conventional
development models.
We are seeking to unlock new forms of
finance through responsible valuation of
our natural assets, our ocean assets
while exploring the potential of
frontier technologies such as quantum
science.
We will form the right partnerships. We
will direct innovation towards our
priorities. But the Pacific's data
ocean, biodiversity, critical minerals,
and traditional knowledge must not power
the next technological revolution while
returning only a fraction of their value
to our people.
Mr. President, from experience, Tonga
knows its challenges and we will meet
them with determination that has always
defined our people. We also know our
strengths as a boss. We are not asking
for charity. We will do our part. We
will simply ask that others do theirs.
Meet the 1.5° C threshold. Help us
protect the planet we all share and the
ocean that connects us. Ensure that
everyone benefit benefits from
technological advancements.
recognize the imbalance between the
funds we commit to addressing our
collective development challenges and
those we are prepared to spend on
conflict.
Let's uphold the rules and institutions
that allow every nation to participate
as an equal sovereign.
That is the promise at the heart of the
United Nations.
Not that all nations would be equal in
power, but that no nation, however
powerful, is more sovereign than
another.
That is the multilateral system. Tonga
believes in an international rules-based
order founded on the UN charter and
equality of nations. And that is the
multilateral system we must preserve.
Mr. President, I so submit. God bless us
all. Maloito,
on behalf of the assembly, I wish to
thank uh the prime minister of the
Kingdom of Tonga.
